THE LIFE OF AARAV MEHTA
A fictional long-form biography and field journal created for testing document question-answering and RAG systems.
All people, organisations, places and events in this document are fictional. Dates and facts are internally consistent where stated.

Part 1 — Beginnings
Aarav Mehta was born on 14 February 1994 in Pune, Maharashtra. His mother, Kavita, taught biology at a municipal secondary school, and his father, Mahesh, repaired electrical motors in a small workshop near the old market. His younger sister, Tara, was born on 3 September 1998. The family lived in a two-bedroom flat above a stationery shop. Aarav's first school was Saraswati Vidya Mandir, where he was quiet in class but curious about how everyday objects worked. His grandfather, Dinesh, gave him a brass compass when he turned nine. Aarav kept it for the rest of his childhood and later carried it on his first long train journey.

Part 2 — School Years
Aarav attended Vidya Vikas Junior College after completing school. He was strongest in physics and English, but his mathematics marks varied. In 2011 he won a district-level science exhibition prize for a hand-built rain gauge. His project partner was Nisha Rao, who later became a civil engineer. The prize was a second-hand camera, not a cash award. During these years Aarav volunteered on Saturdays at the Prerna Reading Room, where he read aloud to children and repaired damaged books. He first met Kabir Sen there. Kabir was two years older and wanted to become a documentary filmmaker.

Part 3 — University
In 2012 Aarav moved to Ahmedabad to study industrial design at the Western Institute of Design. He graduated in 2016 with a Bachelor of Design. His final-year project explored repairable household products. His supervisor was Professor Mira Kulkarni. Aarav's closest university friends were Leela Thomas and Dev Malhotra. He rented a room in a shared house on Navrangpura Road and travelled to campus by bus. He did not receive a university gold medal; he received a commendation for socially useful design. In his final semester he organised a small exhibition called Things Worth Fixing.

Part 4 — First Job
Aarav joined Nivara Appliances in Jaipur in July 2016 as a junior product designer. His first manager was Anita Fernandes. The company made fans, water purifiers and compact kitchen equipment. Aarav worked on a purifier filter housing that could be opened without a special tool. The revised housing reduced service time in a small field trial, although the company never published a formal percentage. In 2018 he moved to Kochi to work for HarbourWorks, a social enterprise that supported coastal livelihoods. He left Nivara on good terms and kept in touch with Anita.

Part 5 — The Turning Point
In August 2019 Aarav visited three villages near Alappuzha with Dr. Sameer Bhat, an environmental engineer. They found that residents received water-quality reports too late to respond to seasonal changes. Aarav proposed a simple monitoring kit with replaceable test strips and a paper logbook. This became Project Riverwatch. The first pilot began in February 2020 with twelve households and one local school. It did not use an artificial-intelligence model. Results were recorded by volunteers and reviewed monthly by Dr. Bhat. The pilot was delayed during the first pandemic lockdown, then resumed in September 2020.

Part 6 — Building a Small Organisation
In March 2021 Aarav and Leela Thomas registered a not-for-profit initiative called CommonCurrent. Its purpose was to help neighbourhood groups design practical, maintainable public-interest projects. Aarav became programme lead, while Leela handled partnerships and accounts. The organisation began with four regular volunteers: Kabir Sen, Farah Qureshi, Rohan Iyer and Nisha Rao. Its first office was a rented room above a bicycle shop in Kochi. The team agreed that every project needed a maintenance plan, a named local owner and a public record of costs. They rejected a proposed project when nobody could explain who would repair its equipment after the grant ended.

Part 7 — Family and Personal Life
Aarav married Leela Thomas on 18 December 2021 in a small ceremony in Kochi. They had first met at university, lost touch for a year, and reconnected at a design workshop in 2018. They have one child, Mira, born on 22 June 2024. The family moved to Bengaluru in January 2023 because CommonCurrent opened a partnership office there. Aarav's mother Kavita retired from teaching in 2022. His father Mahesh continued repairing motors part-time until 2025. Aarav enjoys sketching street scenes and cycling before sunrise. He dislikes being described as a visionary and prefers the phrase practical organiser.

Part 8 — Projects and Outcomes
CommonCurrent later ran several projects. Project Lantern tested solar study lamps in two schools in 2022; the lamps were selected for ease of repair, not brightness alone. Project Seedbank began in 2023 with a network of six gardeners and a seed register maintained on paper. Project OpenShelf started in 2024 using a refurbished delivery van, which visited five schools every fortnight. Project Stepstone paired volunteer mentors with young adults seeking their first technical or trade job. Project RepairCircle held monthly repair days and recorded whether each item was fixed, reused for parts or safely recycled. Project BlueRoof began as a rainwater harvesting pilot in 2025. Project NightBus remained a proposal and was never launched.

Part 9 — Difficult Decisions
In 2022 a donor offered CommonCurrent a large grant on the condition that the organisation use a proprietary monitoring platform. Aarav and Leela declined because the platform required an annual subscription and the local groups would not own their data. The decision created a cash-flow problem, and the organisation froze recruitment for six months. In 2023 a Project Lantern supplier delivered batteries that failed the team's safety checks. Aarav paused distribution, informed the schools and arranged replacement batteries. The delay damaged the team's relationship with the supplier, but the schools later renewed the pilot. Aarav wrote that a missed deadline could be repaired, while a hidden safety issue could destroy trust.

Part 10 — Working Principles
Aarav's notebooks show five recurring principles. First, design for repair rather than replacement. Second, record assumptions separately from measured results. Third, make costs visible to the people who will maintain a project. Fourth, do not describe a pilot as proof of long-term impact. Fifth, give local partners authority to stop work if a safety concern appears. He believes a small project with a reliable maintenance plan can be more useful than a large launch that attracts attention but cannot survive. He is cautious about impressive claims and asks teams to state what they do not know.

Part 11 — Later Work
In 2025 CommonCurrent began documenting its methods so other community groups could reuse them. Aarav led a field guide titled Small Systems, Long Lives, published internally in November 2025. It included checklists for procurement, maintenance, volunteer handover and incident reporting. The guide was not a peer-reviewed academic publication. In April 2026 Aarav began a part-time postgraduate certificate in public systems at the Centre for Civic Practice in Bengaluru. He planned to complete it in 2027. He continued to work four days a week and reserved Fridays for field visits and writing.

Part 12 — Current Priorities
At the beginning of 2027 Aarav's priorities were to stabilise CommonCurrent's finances, complete the BlueRoof evaluation, and hand day-to-day coordination of Project OpenShelf to Farah Qureshi. He wanted to spend more time with his daughter Mira and resume flute lessons. He had not decided whether to expand CommonCurrent to another state. The board asked him to prepare a decision note comparing expansion with strengthening the existing programmes. Aarav's draft argued that expansion should wait until each active project had a documented local owner, a funded maintenance reserve and at least one complete annual review.

PART 13 — CHRONOLOGICAL FIELD JOURNAL
The following dated notes extend the biography with operational details. They are intentionally repetitive in format, as real project archives often are, but each note records a different combination of place, activity, observation and decision.

PART 14 — FINAL INDEX AND FACT CHECK NOTES
Aarav Mehta: born 14 February 1994, Pune. Sister: Tara Mehta, born 3 September 1998. Spouse: Leela Thomas; marriage date 18 December 2021. Child: Mira Mehta, born 22 June 2024. Degree: Bachelor of Design, Western Institute of Design, Ahmedabad, graduated 2016. First employer: Nivara Appliances, joined July 2016 in Jaipur. Later employer/partner organisation: HarbourWorks, Kochi, joined 2018. Co-founded CommonCurrent in March 2021 with Leela Thomas. Project Riverwatch pilot began February 2020 with twelve households and one school. Project NightBus was proposed but never launched. Small Systems, Long Lives was an internal field guide published November 2025, not a peer-reviewed paper. Part-time postgraduate certificate began April 2026, planned completion 2027.
